definition: A reaction turned over by a palladium catalyst. Tagged because what poisons the catalyst is a property of the catalyst and not of any one coupling, so a veto about it has one pattern and many rules -- and because this is the condition class the `requires` column of the competes predicate needs, of which this is the first entry.

A reaction whose medium is strongly acidic -- a Lewis acid, mineral acid, POCl3, or acid with heat. Tagged because the acid is almost never a named precursor (AlCl3, ZnCl2, TFA and POCl3 appear in none of these templates), so what it destroys is invisible to both selectivity channels: each counts distinct products, and a group cleaved off by the medium yields no product to count. MC 42 is the exception and does name its acid, and is included anyway because the chemistry is identical and no forward rule describes the cleavage.

A reaction whose turning point is a carbanion or a carbanion-like organometallic -- a Grignard, an aryllithium from directed metalation, an acetylide. Tagged for the reason `palladium` is: what destroys the intermediate is a property of the intermediate and not of any one reaction. Any protic hydrogen quenches it, so the veto has one pattern and many rules, and the second rule family to need those rows is what earned the tag -- B 20 to B 22 named six Grignard codes explicitly, and an aryllithium is quenched harder.

A reaction whose halogen comes from a reagent rather than from a precursor -- SOCl2, PBr3, POCl3, NBS, Br2, NCS. Tagged because the halogen source *is* the reaction: a free alcohol or an open aryl position sits in most pots, so without this class every one of them reads as a potential halogenation. It is the reagent that is absent, not the substrate.

A reaction driven by an activated acyl, sulfonyl, silyl, trityl or alkyl electrophile supplied as a reagent -- Ac2O, Boc2O, TFAA, MsCl, TsCl, Tf2O, TMSCl, TBSCl, DMTrCl, BnBr, MeI. These are protections and activations, and the reagent is in the pot only when it is the one being used. Coarse on purpose: an Ac2O pot will admit a TBS protection, which is a bounded over-reading and a useful one -- a free hydroxyl beside an activating reagent is worth a peak.

A protecting group removed by a medium the substrate does not carry and no other class names -- fluoride for a silyl ether, hydrazine for a phthalimide, mild base for an acetate or a trifluoroacetamide. The acid-labile groups are `strong-acid` and the hydrogenolysed ones are `reductant`; this is the remainder rather than a category of its own.

A reaction run in aqueous acid or base, with water or hydroxide as the reagent -- ester and nitrile hydrolysis. Separate from `strong-acid`, which is about an anhydrous forcing medium, and tagged because an ester is present in a great many pots while aqueous hydroxide is not.

A reaction needing an oxidant the pot does not otherwise contain -- a chromium or hypervalent-iodine reagent, a peroxide, DMSO/oxalyl chloride. One class for every oxidant rather than one per reagent: the gate tests set containment with no hierarchy, so splitting them would stop an oxidation competing in a pot that holds a different oxidant, which is a finer claim than this table can support.

A reaction turned over by a reducing medium -- a borohydride or aluminium hydride, hydrogen over a metal, a dissolving metal, a phosphine. One class for the same reason `oxidant` is one: `hydride` and `hydrogenation` as separate tags would each fail to be admitted by the other's pot, which asserts more than is known. Reductive amination belongs here even though both its partners are precursors, because without the reductant the reaction stops at the imine.

A reaction turned over by a copper catalyst -- CuAAC, Chan-Lam or Ullmann-type N-arylation. Separate from `palladium` for the reason that one exists: the catalyst is either in the pot or it is not, and the two are not interchangeable.

A reaction needing a condensing or activating agent to join two groups that would otherwise only form a salt -- a carbodiimide or uronium salt for an amide, DIAD and a phosphine for a Mitsunobu. An acid-catalysed esterification is *not* one of these -- it needs acid and the removal of water, which is `strong-acid` and `dehydrating` -- and the difference is testable: a condensing agent takes up the oxygen, so a row declaring this class cannot also shed water. The most common competitor shape in this table is an acid and an amine in one pot; without this class every one of them reads as an amide coupling.

A reaction whose nucleophile is an inorganic salt supplied as a reagent -- azide, cyanide. The substrate side is an ordinary leaving group present in many pots, so the salt is what decides whether the reaction can run at all.

A reaction needing a dehydrating agent or forcing thermal conditions to expel water or carbon dioxide -- a primary amide to a nitrile, a decarboxylation, a heterocycle condensed from a carboxylic acid. Tagged because the substrate alone never says the conditions were there.
